summary: Provides a mechanism by which FTP clients can discover which new features a given FTP server supports, through a FEAT command and an option negotiation.

eli5.summary: A way for a file-fetching program to ask the server, what special things can you do?

questions: how to list ftp server features
what is the ftp feat command
what is the ftp opts command
subtitle: Two FTP commands, FEAT and OPTS, let a client discover what a server supports and choose options.

tldr.problem: FTP keeps gaining new commands, but servers do not all implement every extension, and a client would otherwise have to try each command to find out.
tldr.mechanism: The FEAT command makes the server list the extensions it supports, one per line, and the OPTS command lets the client set options for a later command.
tldr.outcome: A client can learn a server's capabilities in one exchange. A server that errors on FEAT may still support older extensions, so clients should test those individually.

today: RFC 2389 is a Proposed Standard. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
FTP is extended from time to time with new commands and facilities, and implementations cannot be assumed to adopt each one at once. RFC 2389 amends FTP (RFC 959) by adding two commands, FEAT and OPTS.

Together they let a client discover which optional commands a server supports and how, and select among options that any FTP command may support. The RFC uses the key words of BCP 14 (RFC 2119) and the ABNF of RFC 2234. It adds a TCHAR token (visible characters, space or tab) and notes that any reply, including to QUIT, may be multiline unless stated otherwise.
sections.eli5: Servers learn new tricks over time. These two commands let your program ask what tricks a server knows, and ask it to use one in a certain way.

sections.title: The FEAT Command
sections.content:
FEAT takes no parameters. It asks the server to list every extension command or mechanism it supports, meaning anything not defined in RFC 959 or this document, in the form specified by the document that defines the extension. Clients must expect unknown features in the list. That is not an error; it means the server implements something the client has never heard of.

The rationale is traffic and safety. Without FEAT, a client would have to try each extension in turn, which wastes exchanges and may not be possible, since issuing a command just to test for it could have an unwanted effect.

FEAT itself is not listed. Support for it is shown by any reply other than 500 or 502. A server that implements FEAT MUST list all properly documented extensions beyond RFC 959, including ones that predate FEAT, so a client can treat the list as complete.
sections.eli5: Instead of poking every button on a gadget to see what it does, you ask it for a list of its buttons.

sections.title: FEAT Reply Format
sections.content:
A reply is an error response, a single-line 211 no-features reply, or a feature listing. A listing starts with 211- and free-form text (which has no practical use and is not meant for end users). Each feature then sits on its own line that begins with exactly one space, and the listing ends with 211 End. The leading space is required even when there is no ambiguity, because it guarantees a feature line is never mistaken for the end of the listing.

A feature is a label, optionally followed by a space and parameters. The label need not be a command name, and a feature need not add a command. Labels and parameters are nominally case sensitive, though their defining documents usually make them case independent, and implementations are recommended to send upper case. The order of features is unimportant.

A server that does not support FEAT answers 500 or 502, and a syntax error such as giving parameters gets 501. A server that supports FEAT but has no extensions SHOULD send the 211 no-features reply, which MUST be a single line, though a 500 or 502 MAY be used because the two cases are practically indistinguishable.

Several extensions were in widespread use before FEAT existed. An error reply to FEAT therefore does not prove those extensions are missing, and clients should test for them individually.
sections.eli5: The server answers with a tidy list, one item per line, each line starting with a space, and a closing line that says End.

sections.title: The OPTS Command
sections.content:
OPTS lets the client set how the server behaves when another command (the target command) is issued later. It has the form opts SP command-name [ SP command-options ]. The exact syntax and behavior of the options come from the definition of the target command. If none is defined, that command has no options.

The server replies 200 when it recognizes the command name and the options and finds them appropriate. Otherwise it sends 501 for a permanent error, where repeating the command without other changes would fail again, or 451 for a temporary server-side condition that might clear later. An unrecognized OPTS gets 500 or 502.

Any server that implements FEAT MUST implement OPTS, so FEAT does not list it. Neither command has optional functionality, so there is no OPTS FEAT or OPTS OPTS.
sections.eli5: Once you know a button exists, OPTS lets you say how you want it to work next time, like choosing the volume before pressing play.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC believes no significant new security issues, beyond those already in FTP, are created. It admits one side effect: users can learn what a server can do, and may deduce more from it. The same facts could be found by probing for each extension command, but probing may reveal the attacker through logged attempts. The RFC does not consider this serious enough to need a remedy.

The security of features reported by FEAT and set by OPTS should be handled in the documents that define those features.
sections.eli5: Asking what a server can do tells a snooper a bit about it, but guessing would be noisier. The authors decided that was fine.

data.title: FEAT example
data.code:
C> feat
S> 211-Extensions supported:
S>  MLST size*;create;modify*;perm;media-type
S>  SIZE
S>  COMPRESSION
S>  MDTM
S> 211 END
